CHRISTOPHER HERRMANN
INT. LEARNING    REFLECTIONS    RESUME   


R1 - EE576: High Voltage Engineering

A misnomer and retrospection


When I enrolled in Dr. Burke’s EE576 High Voltage Engineering class I was skeptical, but open minded. In this class we covered the fundamentals of electrical grids, high voltage generation, grid scale technologies and trends, and of course, the age old debate between AC and DC power. Despite what one may glean from the history books, this debate is not over, and the historic underdog may still have its day! Despite these interesting topics and a deep-rooted initiative to learn, I came away from the class ultimately unchanged in my preferences, and that’s okay.

To start, I had two different reasons to enroll in this class: a misnomer, and a decision. Considering this would be one of my first classes of my graduate degree while also working full time, my choices for classes were mainly motivated by scheduling. Nevertheless, I thought to myself “High voltage engineering, that sounds useful!” Considering at the time of enrollment I was beginning to work with high voltage motor drives, this seemed like a great augmentation to my professional knowledge. The course description even included the phrase “electrical shock and safety.” Some of the projects I had been assigned at my job operated at over 300 volts, so this was a reassuring inclusion for a newly graduated EE.

Despite high hopes, I quickly realized that this course would not include fundamental high voltage circuit design, guide me towards building my own electric car, or explain how to shoot magnificent bolts of lighting from my fingertips as a weekend project. Instead, this class was mostly geared as an introduction to those interested in the noble and esteemed field of grid-scale power systems. Hence, my declaration of a misnomer. In retrospect, a better title for the course may have been “Electrical Grids and You: An Introduction.”

I don’t mean to give the wrong impression of my respect for the field. Grid-scale electrical engineering is absolutely fundamental to our modern way of life. I am eternally grateful to the engineers who toil away over kilometer spanning simulations, and have nightmares about grid stability and power factors. Just a few months before, I had already made the decision that I was not interested in becoming one of those esteemed engineers. Which brings us to my “decision.”

The summer prior to my graduation, I had the luxury of being offered two summer internships. The first offer was from a Buffalo-based aerospace company, where I would be writing firmware and designing circuits for high performance motion control. The second offer was from a well known company in my hometown. This opportunity involved managing the sprawling grid inter-connects that they relied on for their production lines and research facilities. During my interview for the latter I was given two key takeaways: 1) I would be responsible for directly negotiating with the local power company. 2) In this line of work, there is zero room for failure.

I know that I learn best by doing. Unfortunately for me, “doing” is often synonymous with “failing.” In different circumstances, this type of learning process can even be considered an asset. We don’t grow as people or engineers unless we are willing to try new things and step outside our comfort zone, and failure is an integral part of that process. Considering that my interviewer felt it necessary to point out that there is zero room for failure, this situation felt somewhat incompatible with that mentality. I chose to stay in Buffalo for the summer.

Of course, every field of electrical engineering is multi-faceted. With only a single data point about the engineering involved with grid-scale power engineering, I was ready to approach EE574 with an open mind. This came with some personal discomfort. What if I discovered some fascinating topic that made me question my first major career decision? In a way, this class was a reckoning of my first and only professional decision to date.

We covered a wide range of topics in Dr. Burke’s class. This included the mundane discussion of different types of transmission line towers and components, to the surprisingly dramatic, contemporary evolution to the Edison v. Tesla debate: What’s better, alternating current or direct current? My favorite part of the class though, was definitely the final project, where students presented on the high voltage engineering topic of their choice. I chose to present on different types of particle accelerators, because they are some of the most power hungry machines on the grid today, but may be the ultimate answer to clean, limitless energy via fusion.

In essence, the grid is just one gigantic circuit, or in the case of the US, multiple gigantic circuits. And just like any other circuit it’s made up of components.

I find it interesting that many of these components are performing the same fundamental functions in the same way they did 100 years ago. Of course, there have been improvements in materials, monitoring capability, load balancing, etc. But in a way a lot of things remain the same as they were a century ago. These systems are huge, slow moving, and very risk adverse. Nevertheless, the grid is changing, and it looks like Tesla may not be the victor in the long run.

Many people are at least somewhat familiar with the “War of the Currents” that took place in the late 1800s. Broadly speaking, as cities continued to electrify, there was fierce debate and competition over the best way to deliver power to paying customers: alternating current or direct current. Proponents of direct current included Thomas Edision, who had made significant investments into building DC-based infrastructure. While the main champion of AC current was George Westinghouse, whose company relied on the technical foundation that had been laid and licensed from Nikola Tesla. Plugging in a hairdryer, TV, or other appliance it’s clear that Westinghouse and Tesla ultimately won this battle thanks to the superior efficiency, and thus, range of transmission that alternating current enabled at the time. But while they may have won the battle, the war is not over.

The modern power generation and consumption landscape is much more complicated than it was in the late 1800s. Professor Burke explained that the addition of renewable energy sources like wind and solar, as well as the rise of more advanced, high voltage semiconductors has actually made large scale DC power transmission much more economical. At the risk of over simplifying, the core argument in support of high voltage DC transmission is that you can simply use “more of the wire” than with a comparable AC transmission system.

Whenever alternating current is involved within a circuit, the “skin effect” comes into play. Without delving into the physics, this effect manifests as the tendency for alternating current to flow non-uniformly through the cross section of the conductor, with the highest current density being focused along the outside of the conductor i.e. the skin. This means that the diameter of the conductor is effectively reduced, limiting the amount of alternating current it can safely carry. Obviously, this is very undesirable as power companies still need to pay the price for the “whole” wire even though a portion of it is effectively dead weight.

This issue doesn’t exist for high voltage direct current transmission, meaning that pound-for-pound, a wire carrying direct current is much more efficient, thus cheaper. Further, wires carrying direct current transmission wires can handle peak voltages that are up to 50% higher than with AC systems, meaning they need to carry less current and again, boosting their efficiency.

The conclusion of the class, of course, was a final presentation on the topic of our choice. I really enjoyed the freedom that Dr. Burke allowed us, with almost any high voltage topic being fair game, pending his approval. I immensely enjoyed listening to the variety of topics that the presentations covered, although some were more interesting than others. Having worked at the Cornell High Energy Synchrotron Source a few summers previously, my presentation was focused on particle accelerators. Even the simplest particle accelerators consume massive amounts of power and rely on high voltages to accelerate and steer particles moving at a significant fraction of the speed of light. Considering the CHESS facility was responsible for approximately 30% of Cornell’s power bill, and required its own dedicated substation connection, I figured this was an appropriate topic.

With all of this fascinating content still fresh in my mind, the question remained: Was it time to change careers? The verdict: No.

I will give myself some credit in that I approached this class with an open mind, despite my initial feeling that I had been deceived. By taking this class, I was attempting to actively question my preconceived notions. At the end of the class I had developed a refreshed appreciation for the infrastructure and engineers that are largely invisible to us, yet enable every aspect of our daily life. The topics covered in this class are fundamental to the technology and expertise that literally billions of people rely on every single day. I can safely assert that I want no part in it.

While the scale of electrical grids across the world is staggering and ever changing, this class reaffirmed my conclusion that this field is not a good fit for me. While there I have no doubt that innovation is constantly happening within this field, concrete changes are rightfully slow and meticulous. I prefer to fail fast and learn faster. I like to get my hands dirty with circuits on my bench and a soldering iron in my hand. So while I found the topics interesting, I don’t think a career change is in my near future. Sometimes knowing what you don’t like is just as important as finding your true passion.
